heroIntro: Selling land in Bangladesh while you live in the UK, USA, Canada or the EU depends on one document: a power of attorney that survives every checkpoint from a foreign notary to a Sub-Registrar in Bangladesh. This pillar guide walks through the full chain, including drafting, signing abroad, Embassy or High Commission attestation, MOFA verification in Dhaka, stamp duty, registration, buyer due diligence, revocation and fraud red flags. It is written by Advocate Md. Shah Alam, Supreme Court of Bangladesh. For case-specific help call or WhatsApp the chamber on 01712655546, or start at the NRB legal help hub.

Have the deed attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission and ask whether a preliminary local authentication is required first.
MOFA Dhaka verification of the Mission attestation is commonly expected; confirm with the Sub-Registry whether it is required in your case.
The agent presents the POA and the sale deed to the Sub-Registrar under sections 32 and 33 of the Registration Act 1908, and the sale deed must be registered.
Stamp duty, attestation and registration fees change, so check the current fee schedule with each office.
Revoke the POA in writing after the sale, and treat any rush, secrecy or mismatched documents as fraud red flags.

sections.h2: Why a Power of Attorney From Abroad Is the Riskiest Document in a Land Sale
sections.content:
For most non-resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) in the UK, USA, Canada or the EU, a land sale in Bangladesh cannot wait for a personal visit. The usual solution is a power of attorney (POA, also called mukhtarnama or attorney deed) in favour of a trusted relative or lawyer. The same document that makes the sale possible is also the document most often used to defraud absent owners.

The reason is simple: the Sub-Registrar who registers a sale deed never meets you. He or she relies on a paper trail that begins in a foreign notary's office, passes through a Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission, and ends in Dhaka. If any link in that chain is weak, the buyer's title can be challenged years later, often at the exact moment the property has become valuable or a family dispute has started.

This guide follows the whole chain end to end: drafting, signing abroad, consular attestation, Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) verification in Dhaka, stamp duty, registration under the Registration Act 1908, buyer due diligence, revocation risk and fraud red flags. For shorter overviews, see our guides on POA for property from abroad and POA for land transfer. For the wider picture of services for Bangladeshis overseas, visit the NRB legal help hub.

Disclaimer: This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Statutes, forms, fees, consular rules and registry practice change and differ between countries and offices. Confirm the current requirements with the relevant Bangladesh Mission, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Sub-Registrar's office, and consult a qualified advocate before you sign or rely on any document.

sections.h2: The Full Chain at a Glance: From Your Desk Abroad to the Sub-Registry
sections.content:
A POA executed abroad becomes usable for a land sale only after it clears several checkpoints. The exact requirements differ by country and by office, so treat the table below as a map, not as a rulebook.

StageWho is involvedWhat happensWhat to verify
1. DraftingAdvocate in Bangladesh (preferably) and youDeed is drafted in clear terms naming the land, the agent and the exact powersLand details match the latest records; powers are specific, not vague
2. Signing abroadNotary public, or a consular officer of the Bangladesh MissionYou sign in person, with identity checked, and the notary or officer authenticates itName spelling matches your passport and your land records; every page is initialled
3. Mission attestationBangladesh Embassy or High CommissionThe Mission verifies the notary's signature and seal, or records its own authenticationWhether a prior step (such as local foreign-ministry authentication) is required first
4. MOFA verificationMinistry of Foreign Affairs, Dhaka (consular or attestation section)Mission attestation is checked and countersigned for use inside BangladeshWhether the receiving Sub-Registry currently insists on it; current procedure and fee
5. Stamp and registrationYour agent, the Sub-Registrar, and the buyerAgent presents the POA, and later the sale deed, for registrationStamp paid correctly; POA registered or recognised under the Registration Act 1908
6. Post-sale stepsBuyer and assistant commissioner (land)Mutation (namjari) and record updatesDeed number, volume and date are recorded correctly

Notice that the buyer's lawyer will check each of these steps. If you are the seller, a POA that is complete and well documented will make your buyer more confident and can help the deal complete faster.

sections.h2: The Legal Framework: Powers of Attorney Act 1882, Registration Act 1908 and Related Laws
sections.content:
Several statutes work together. You do not need to memorise them, but your advocate should be able to explain how each applies to your file.

  • Powers-of-Attorney Act 1882: deals with how a person holding a power of attorney may execute documents and act for the principal, and gives certain protections to those who act in good faith. Read the current text with your advocate for the exact provisions.
  • Contract Act 1872 (agency provisions): an agent's authority can end when the principal revokes it (section 201 deals with termination of agency), and revocation takes effect against third persons only when it becomes known to them (section 208). This is why revocation must be communicated and, ideally, registered.
  • Registration Act 1908, sections 32 and 33: section 32 lists who may present a document for registration, including an agent holding a power of attorney. Section 33 sets out which powers of attorney the registering officer must recognise. For a principal who lives outside Bangladesh, a power of attorney executed before and authenticated by a notary public, a court, a judge, a magistrate or a Bangladesh consular representative is of the kind the section contemplates. Ask your advocate to confirm the current wording and any amendments.
  • Transfer of Property Act 1882, section 54: a sale of immovable property of the value prescribed in that section can be made only by a registered instrument. A sale deed signed by an agent still has to be registered.
  • Evidence Act 1872, section 85: courts presume that a power of attorney executed before and authenticated by a notary public, court, judge, magistrate or consular officer was duly executed. That presumption is useful in later litigation but can still be rebutted by proof of forgery or fraud.
  • Stamp Act 1899 and the Penal Code 1860: the first governs stamp duty on the deed, and the second punishes cheating and forgery (for example sections 420, 467, 468 and 471).

One practical point: the statutes do not use the words "MOFA verification". That step comes from administrative practice and government circulars, which is why it can change. Always ask the Sub-Registry and the Mission what they require at the moment you start.

sections.h2: Step 1: Drafting the POA - Special or General, and the Clauses That Matter
sections.content:
Most disputes begin with a badly drafted deed. If you are selling one specific plot, a special power of attorney is usually safer than a general one. Our guide to POA types and registration explains the difference in detail.

A strong land-sale POA normally contains:

  • Full identity of the principal: name as in your passport, father's and mother's names, Bangladeshi NID or old passport details where available, current foreign address and nationality. Mismatches between spellings are a leading cause of rejection.
  • Full identity of the agent: name, parentage, NID number, address and relationship to you.
  • Exact schedule of property: district, upazila, mouza, plot (dag) numbers by each survey record (CS, SA, RS, BS as applicable), khatian numbers, area, boundaries and how you acquired the land. Copy these from the latest records, not from memory.
  • Specific powers: to negotiate, to receive earnest money, to sign the sale agreement and the sale deed, to appear before the Sub-Registrar, to admit execution, to receive the price, to apply for mutation, and to pay taxes. If you do not want the agent to receive money, say so and arrange payment into your own account.
  • Price floor or conditions: a minimum price, an approved buyer, or a requirement for your written approval before the final deed. This is your best protection against under-value sales.
  • Duration and revocation language: a clear end date or event, and a statement that you may revoke the deed.
  • Caution on "irrevocable" clauses: these draw heavy scrutiny. Do not use them unless an advocate has explained the consequences, especially where money has been paid to you.

Draft the deed in Bangladesh with your advocate, send it to you as a PDF, and print it on plain paper abroad for signing. Do not accept a half-filled template from a broker. For a clean transfer, also see our overview of legal checks for buying land from abroad, which a buyer's lawyer will use against your documents.

sections.h2: Step 2: Signing Abroad Before a Notary or Consular Officer
sections.content:
You have two routes. Which is better depends on the country where you live and the Mission's current services.

Route A: Sign before a local notary public. You appear in person with passport or national identity, sign in front of the notary, and the notary signs, stamps and records the act. In the UK this is usually a notary public or solicitor with notarial powers; in the USA it may be a notary public with state-specific rules; in Canada, a notary or a lawyer who is a commissioner. This route is common because notaries are easy to find.

Route B: Sign directly before the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission. Many Missions can authenticate a deed signed before their consular officer. This often shortens the chain because the Mission's own authentication replaces the foreign notary and the later check of the notary's seal. Whether the Mission offers it, whether an appointment is needed, and what fee applies are matters to confirm directly with the Mission.

Whichever route you choose:

  • Sign only in front of the notary or officer. Never pre-sign.
  • Bring your valid passport and, if possible, documents showing your Bangladeshi identity (NID, old passport, birth certificate).
  • Initial every page and make sure any annexed land schedule is attached and referred to in the main deed.
  • Ask that the deed be in English, or in Bengali with an accurate English translation, according to the Mission's rules. If a translation is required, use a competent translator and keep the certificate.
  • Ask for the notary's registry or serial number and keep a copy of the full signed set.

sections.h2: Step 3: Embassy or High Commission Attestation
sections.content:
If you signed before a foreign notary, the next stage is attestation by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission that covers your country. The Mission does not rewrite or approve the contents of your deed. It authenticates the signature and seal of the notary or the foreign authority, so that offices in Bangladesh can trust the document's origin.

Points to confirm with your Mission before you travel or post documents:

  • Prior authentication: some Missions ask that the notary's signature first be authenticated by a local government body, such as a foreign ministry, a state authority or a county office. Requirements differ by country, so ask rather than assume.
  • Apostille is not the same as consular attestation: an apostille is a certificate under an international convention, and it is a different process from consular attestation. Do not assume that an apostille alone satisfies a Bangladesh office. Ask the Mission whether it is needed as a preliminary step.
  • Appointment, mailing and original documents: whether you must appear in person, whether postal submission is accepted, and whether originals or photocopies are needed.
  • Fees: check the current fee schedule on the Mission's website. Do not rely on agents' quoted amounts.
  • Return of the document: how and to whom the attested deed will be handed back or couriered.

Keep the attestation page, the notary's page and the deed together as one bound set. Loose attachments cause suspicion at the registry.

After attestation abroad, the document is sent to Bangladesh. Many registry offices, banks and courts expect the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Dhaka to verify the Mission's attestation and add its own stamp or signature, confirming that the Mission's seal and the officer's signature are genuine. This is often what people mean by "MOFA attestation".

Practical points:

  • Who submits: usually your agent, a lawyer or a representative, using the original attested set. Ask the ministry whether authorisation or ID is required from the person submitting.
  • Timing and fee: processing times and fees are set by the ministry and may change. Check the current fee schedule and expected time before relying on any date.
  • Is it always required? Practice varies between sub-registry offices and also depends on the purpose. For a land sale, a prudent plan is to complete MOFA verification unless the Sub-Registry and your advocate confirm in writing that it is not needed for your case.
  • Keep copies: make colour scans of the deed, the notary page, the Mission page and the MOFA page before anything is submitted.

Where the deed was signed directly before a consular officer, the pathway may be shorter. The exact route is a question for both the Mission and the ministry, so confirm in advance rather than discover a missing step on the day of registration.

sections.h2: Stamp Requirements and Registration With the Sub-Registrar
sections.content:
The deed must carry the stamp duty (non-judicial stamp) required under the Stamp Act 1899 and the current schedule. The amount depends on the type of deed and how it is structured, for example whether it covers one or several agents and one or several properties. I am deliberately not quoting a figure because schedules and e-stamp arrangements change. Ask your advocate or the registry to compute it and check the current fee schedule.

A deed executed abroad is often stamped after it arrives in Bangladesh, within the period allowed by the stamp law. Ask your advocate about the time limit and the correct procedure so that the deed does not become liable to penalty.

Then comes the registry:

  1. Registration of the POA: for a POA that authorises the sale of land, registry offices expect it to be registered or at least presented for recognition under section 33 of the Registration Act. The Sub-Registrar examines the notary or consular authentication and the attestation chain.
  2. Presentation of the sale deed: the agent signs the sale deed in your name as attorney, and presents it under section 32 along with the POA. Identification of the agent is checked, and registry staff usually take photographs and fingerprints or biometric data under the current system.
  3. Payment of registration fee and taxes: registration fee, source tax, local government tax and other charges as presently prescribed. Check the current fee schedule on the day.
  4. Return of the registered deed: keep the receipt and later obtain the certified copy.
  5. Mutation (namjari): the buyer then applies for mutation. Our guide to mutation from abroad explains the usual steps.

Which Sub-Registry has jurisdiction is determined by where the land is situated. Registration in the wrong office can be a basis for challenge, so confirm this before you book a date.

sections.h2: Step-by-Step Checklist: POA From Abroad for a Land Sale
sections.content:
Use this as a working checklist, and tick off each line only when you hold the document in your hand.

  1. Collect the land documents: deed of ownership, latest khatian, mutation record, land development tax receipts, and any heirship certificate if the land was inherited.
  2. Appoint an advocate in Bangladesh to verify the title and to prepare the draft POA.
  3. Decide on the agent. Choose someone reliable and, preferably, a person who is not in a conflict of interest with you.
  4. Fix the powers: special POA for one specific sale, with a price floor and a ban on any other transaction.
  5. Review the draft carefully and check every spelling against your passport and land records.
  6. Print the final text, then sign in person before a notary public or a consular officer abroad.
  7. Obtain any preliminary authentication required by the Mission (confirm in writing or by email).
  8. Submit the deed for Embassy or High Commission attestation and pay the fee shown on the Mission's site.
  9. Courier the full attested set to your agent and keep scanned copies and tracking records.
  10. Have MOFA Dhaka verify the attestation, unless your advocate confirms in writing that it is not necessary.
  11. Pay the stamp duty and have the POA registered or presented for recognition at the proper Sub-Registry.
  12. Agree the sale in writing with the buyer, with part-payment into your bank account or by an auditable route.
  13. Have the sale deed registered under sections 32 and 33 of the Registration Act and receive the receipt.
  14. Obtain the certified copy of the registered deed and confirm that the buyer has applied for mutation.
  15. Arrange lawful remittance of proceeds through banking channels and check with Bangladesh Bank rules or a bank officer on repatriation requirements.
  16. Revoke the POA formally once the transaction is complete, and send written notice to the agent.

sections.h2: Comparison Table: Four Ways to Authorise a Land Sale From Abroad
sections.content:
A POA is not the only option. This table compares the main routes at a high level; your advocate can tell you which fits your property, family and timeline.

RouteStrengthsWeaknessesBest used when
Special POA signed before a foreign notary, then Mission attestation and MOFA verificationCommon, flexible, widely understood by registriesMore steps, more documents to match, forgery risk if drafting is looseYou live abroad and need to sell one defined property
Special POA signed before a Bangladesh consular officerFewer checkpoints; authentication by the Mission itselfDepends on the Mission's services and appointment availabilityThe Mission near you offers this service and you can travel there
General POA covering all your Bangladesh affairsOne document for banking, rent, tax and litigationWide authority, high abuse risk; registries may ask for more proof for a saleLong-term management, not a single sale; use with strong safeguards
Signing the deed yourself on a visit to BangladeshNo agent risk, clean registry recordNeeds travel and time in the countryHigh-value land or a contested family property

Where family members share the land, consider also the position of co-heirs, because a sale of the whole by one co-owner or his agent invites dispute. Our guide to types of POA covers the extent of authority in more depth.

sections.h2: Buyer Due Diligence: What a Careful Purchaser Checks
sections.content:
If you are the seller, think like the buyer's lawyer and answer these questions before they are asked. If you are the buyer, insist on each of them.

  • Is the owner alive and does he or she still stand behind the POA? A POA ends on death of the principal. Ask for a recent confirmation, preferably recorded in writing or on a video call that the buyer's lawyer attends, and ask whether there has been any revocation.
  • Does the POA match the land? Compare plot numbers, khatian, mouza and area in the POA with the title deed, the mutation record and the current online record.
  • Was the deed properly authenticated abroad? Look at the notary or consular authentication, the Mission attestation, the MOFA verification and the stamping. Check names, dates and seals for any inconsistency.
  • Is the POA registered, and is there any registered revocation? Ask the relevant Sub-Registry whether a revocation deed has been recorded, and obtain a certified copy of the POA register entry.
  • Does the agent hold the power to receive money? If not, pay only to the owner's bank account.
  • Is the price reasonable? A big gap below market value, or a POA with a very high-speed process, is a warning sign.
  • Are there other claims? Check for pending suits, mortgages, acquisition, vested or abandoned property claims and co-sharer rights. See our buyer checklist.
  • Is the agent's identity genuine? Compare NID, photograph and signature, and be wary of a person who is evasive about how to reach the owner.

Buyers should avoid paying any large sum before the deed is registered. The sale is complete only on registration, and earnest money should be documented in a written agreement with a clear refund clause.

sections.h2: Revocation, Death and Incapacity: How a POA Can Fail After You Sign
sections.content:
A POA is not permanent. Understanding how it ends protects both sides.

  • Revocation by the principal: you can generally revoke the authority of your agent, subject to any legal protection for rights coupled with an interest. To protect yourself, make revocation in writing, register it where the original POA was registered, notify the agent in writing and notify known third parties such as the buyer, banks and the Sub-Registry.
  • Notice to third parties: under the agency rules of the Contract Act, revocation binds a third person only once it is known to that person. Until the buyer knows, the buyer may be protected if he acts in good faith. Unrecorded revocation is therefore risky.
  • Death of the principal: the authority normally ends on the death of the person who granted it. A sale deed signed by an agent after the principal's death, even if both sides are unaware of it, creates serious doubt over title and may be void. Heirs must act quickly to inform the registry and close the file.
  • Unsoundness of mind: if the principal loses capacity, the agent's authority generally ends as well.
  • Completion of the task: a special POA for one sale ends once the sale is complete.
  • Agent's death or resignation: authority also ends on the agent's death or renunciation.
  • Expiry: if the deed contains an end date, it lapses on that date.

If you suspect your agent has acted beyond the powers granted, a civil suit for cancellation of the deed and a prohibitory injunction can be filed under the Specific Relief Act 1877 and the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, and a criminal complaint may be considered where forgery or cheating is suspected. Speed matters, because third-party rights can arise quickly.

sections.h2: Fraud Red Flags and the Reality of Remote or Video Signing
sections.content:
Fraud involving absent owners is a recurring pattern. Watch for the following red flags.

  • Pressure and secrecy: an agent who insists on speed, discourages you from contacting your advocate, or refuses to share copies.
  • Inconsistent documents: a notary seal from one country with a date that does not match the Mission stamp, spelling differences between pages, or pages that look re-typed.
  • A POA you never signed: if someone tells you that a POA exists in your name and you do not remember signing it, treat it as an emergency.
  • Photographs of "you" that are low quality or edited, or a foreign identity paper that cannot be verified.
  • Broker quotes for "fast attestation": middlemen who promise to obtain attestation without your appearance should be avoided. A genuine authentication needs the real participation of the notary or consular officer.
  • Payment to a third-party account: never accept the price into an account that is not yours or that of a clearly authorised person.

Video-call or electronic signing. Many NRBs ask whether they can sign over video. Bangladeshi practice on remote notarisation and electronic signatures on land documents is still evolving, and registry offices differ in how they treat them. Whether a given Mission or ministry accepts a remotely notarised or electronically signed POA must be checked with them directly. If you cannot obtain written confirmation, do not use that method for a land sale. A video call can still be useful for something else: a short recorded confirmation to the buyer's lawyer that you have granted the POA, which supports the paperwork but never replaces it.

If you discover forgery, consult an advocate immediately about a criminal complaint (the Penal Code deals with cheating and forgery, for example sections 420, 467, 468 and 471), a civil suit to cancel the document, and a prompt injunction to stop further transfers.

sections.h2: Common Mistakes NRBs Make With a POA for Land Sale
sections.content:
• Using a template from the internet without a Bangladeshi advocate reviewing the property schedule and the powers.
  • Granting a general POA when only a single sale is intended.
  • Spelling mismatches between the passport, the deed and the land records, leading to rejection or later challenge.
  • Skipping the preliminary authentication that the Mission requires, then discovering the delay after the notary visit.
  • Assuming an apostille or notary seal alone is enough for Bangladesh. The consular attestation step and any ministry verification are separate.
  • Forgetting stamp duty or stamping late, which can bring penalty and delays.
  • No price floor and no buyer approval clause, leaving the agent free to sell low.
  • Giving the agent power to collect all the money with no audit trail.
  • Not revoking the POA after the sale or after losing trust in the agent.
  • Ignoring heirs and co-owners and their rights to the same property.
  • Never checking the registry afterwards for any transaction under your name or for unexpected recorded POAs.

For a smoother process, prepare the full document set in advance and cross-check each name and number against the originals. If you are an NRB with a complex family property or suspect misuse of an existing POA, you can speak to a land lawyer through NRB legal help.

sections.h2: Related Reading and When to Get Legal Help
sections.content:
These guides on this site expand on parts of the process:

  • Power of attorney for Bangladesh property from abroad
  • Power of attorney for land transfer in Bangladesh
  • Types of POA and registration in Bangladesh
  • Land mutation (namjari) from abroad, step by step
  • Buying land in Bangladesh from abroad: legal checklist

Consider engaging an advocate when the property is of high value, when co-heirs exist, when the land has a history of litigation, when you did not personally prepare the POA, or when you suspect that a deed has been used without your consent. A lawyer can verify title, supervise drafting, liaise with the Mission and the ministry, attend registration, and file urgent court applications if needed.

Confirm the current requirements with the relevant Bangladesh Mission, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Sub-Registrar's office, and consult a qualified advocate before you sign or rely on any document.

faqs.question: Can I sell my Bangladesh land from the UK, USA or Canada using a power of attorney?
faqs.answer: Yes, in principle. You execute a POA abroad before a notary or consular officer, have it attested by the Bangladesh Mission, complete any ministry verification in Dhaka, stamp it and have your agent present it to the Sub-Registrar along with the sale deed. The sale deed itself must still be registered.

faqs.question: Is Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission attestation mandatory?
faqs.answer: For a deed signed before a foreign notary, practice in Bangladesh is to require attestation by the Bangladesh Mission so that the notary's signature and seal can be trusted. If you sign directly before a Bangladesh consular officer, the authentication may be performed by the Mission itself. Confirm the current requirement with the Mission and the Sub-Registry.

faqs.question: What is MOFA verification and do I need it?
faqs.answer: It is verification by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Dhaka of the Mission attestation, so that offices inside Bangladesh can rely on it. Practice varies by office and purpose, so ask your advocate to confirm with the Sub-Registry whether it is required for your case. Check the current procedure and fee schedule before you apply.

faqs.question: Does a POA signed abroad have to be registered in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Where the POA authorises sale of land, registry offices expect it to be registered or presented for recognition under sections 32 and 33 of the Registration Act 1908. Ask your advocate how the Sub-Registry handles it at present.

faqs.question: How much stamp duty and what fees will I pay?
faqs.answer: Amounts depend on the type of deed, the number of agents and properties, and on current schedules and e-stamp rules. Check the current fee schedule with the Sub-Registry and the Mission instead of relying on quotes from brokers.

faqs.question: How long does the whole attestation chain take?
faqs.answer: It depends on the country, the Mission's appointment queue, courier time, ministry processing and the registry. No reliable fixed period can be promised, so plan generously and ask each office for its current time frame.

faqs.question: Can I sign a POA over a video call?
faqs.answer: Treat this with caution. Rules on remote notarisation and electronic signatures differ and the Mission, ministry and registry may not accept them. Do not use this route for a land sale unless each of those offices confirms acceptance in writing.

faqs.question: What happens if the owner dies after signing the POA?
faqs.answer: The agent's authority normally ends on the principal's death. A deed signed after death can be challenged as void. Heirs should inform the registry and any buyer immediately and take legal advice.

faqs.question: How do I cancel a POA I gave to a relative?
faqs.answer: Prepare a written deed of revocation, have it executed and authenticated in the proper manner, register it where the original POA was recorded, notify the agent and give written notice to buyers, banks and the Sub-Registry. Revocation binds third persons only once they know of it.

faqs.question: Can the buyer rely on the POA alone?
faqs.answer: A careful buyer will also verify the owner's identity and continuing consent, the match between POA and land records, the registry entry, the absence of any recorded revocation and the payment route. A POA alone is not a guarantee of valid title.
